Inherited from Middle French famille, borrowed from Latin familia.

Inherited from Middle French main, Old French main, mein, man, from Latin manus (“hand”), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry). Compare Spanish mano and Italian mano.

examples.text: L'enfant joue dans le parc.

translations.de: Das Kind spielt im Park.

translations.pt: A criança está brincando no parque.

examples.text: Les enfants sont à l'école.

translations.de: Die Kinder sind in der Schule.
translations.en: The children are at school.
translations.pt: As crianças estão na escola.

more.definition: child (someone who is not yet an adult); child (offspring of any age); son, native (of a place)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French enfant, from Old French enfant, from Latin īnfantem.
From Middle French vieulx, from Old French viel, from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.
From Middle French vieulx, from Old French viel, from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.
Inherited from Latin mātūtīnus (“of the morning”), from Matuta, Roman goddess of morning.
Deverbal from pardonner.
Deverbal from pardonner.

more.definition: result; sequel; next step, next steps, that which follows, remainder, rest
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French suite, from earlier siute, from Vulgar Latin *sequita, (instead of classical secūta), as the feminine past participle of *sequere, from Latin sequi.

more.definition: towards; to; around, circa (with a date or time)
more.etymology: From Latin versus (past participle of vertere). Cognate to Italian verso (preposition). Doublet of versus.

more.definition: confronted with, faced with; in front of, before; outside
more.etymology: From de + avant. False cognate of Indonesian and Malay depan despite similarity of both words in definition and pronunciation.

more.definition: finally; in the end; at last, finally; in fact; indeed
more.etymology: Univerbation of en + fin. Literally, “in the end”.

senses.gloss_en: to cease, to stop, to quit
to balk, to block, to hinder stop, to delay

more.definition: to stop, to come to a standstill; to halt, to stop from moving; to arrest (someone, a criminal, etc.); to stop, to cease (an activity)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French arrester (“to stop”), from Old French arester (“to stay, stop”), from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“stop, remain behind, stay back”). Compare English arrest.
Inherited from Old French cause, borrowed from Classical Latin causa. Compare chose, an inherited doublet.

more.definition: a room.; a hotel room.; a bedroom.
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French chambre, cambre, from Latin cambra, Medieval spelling of Latin camera (“room”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “something with an arched cover: a covered wagon, a covered boat, a vaulted chamber”). Doublet of caméra, a borrowing.

more.definition: right (on the right-hand side); straight (not bent or crooked); right (of an angle)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French droit (spelled dreit in Early Old French, such as the Oaths of Strasbourg), inherited from Late Latin drictus, syncopated form of Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direct. In Middle French, it was for a time spelled droict to reflect the original Latin etymology.

more.definition: straight, straight on; upright, straight, not bent or crooked
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French droit (spelled dreit in Early Old French, such as the Oaths of Strasbourg), inherited from Late Latin drictus, syncopated form of Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direct. In Middle French, it was for a time spelled droict to reflect the original Latin etymology.

more.definition: right (entitlement); law (study of law); right angle
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French droit (spelled dreit in Early Old French, such as the Oaths of Strasbourg), inherited from Late Latin drictus, syncopated form of Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direct. In Middle French, it was for a time spelled droict to reflect the original Latin etymology.

more.definition: divided into two equal parts vertically, per pale; said of an escutcheon; drunk

water, a liquid that is transparent, colorless, odorless, and tasteless in its pure form, the primary constituent of lakes, rivers, seas, and oceans; In particular, rain; the chemical compound with molecular formula H₂O existing in the form of ice, liquid water or steam
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French eau, eaue, from Old French ewe, euwe, egua (“water”), from Latin aqua (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water, flowing water”), related to Frankish *ahu ~ ahwā (“stream, water”). See also English ea (“watercourse, river”).

Inherited from Middle French terre, from Old French terre, from Latin terra (“earth”), from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”). See cognates in regional languages in France: Norman terre; Gallo tèrr or terre; Picard tère; Bourguignon târre; Franco-Provençal and Occitan tèrra; Corsican terra.
Inherited from Latin longē, from the adjective longus (“long, far-off”). Compare Catalan lluny, archaic Spanish lueñe.
Inherited from Old French mari, from Latin marītus.
Unclear, see English fine.

more.definition: end, close, finish; end, end goal, objective, purpose
more.etymology: From Middle French fin, from Old French fin, from Latin finis.

more.definition: to believe (someone); to believe, to accept as true; to believe, to have faith
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French creire, croire, from Latin crēdere. Cognates with Norman creire, Gallo craire, Picard croère, Bourguignon croire, Franco-Provençal crêre, Occitan creire, créser, Corsican credè.

more.definition: big, thick, fat; coarse, rough; famous
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French gros, from Latin grossus.
Deverbal of boulotter, similar semantic development as in -role

more.definition: rather, instead (indicating preference); rather (introducing a correction or clarification); rather, pretty, kind of (indicating intensity or degree)
more.etymology: From Middle French plustost, see plus + tôt. Compare Italian piuttosto and Catalan més aviat. Compare the etymology of English rather.
Inherited from Middle French prest, from Old French prest, from Late Latin praestus, from the Latin adverb praestō. Compare Catalan prest, Italian presto. Doublet of preste.

Inherited from Old French burel, diminutive of *bure (compare Middle French bure (“coarse woolen cloth”), French bourre (“hair, fluff”)), from Late Latin burra (“wool, fluff, shaggy cloth, coarse fabric”); akin to Ancient Greek βερβέριον (berbérion, “shabby garment”).

senses.gloss_en: to die, to perish, to decease, to depart

more.definition: to die; to be dying; to be dying (of); to be dying
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French mourir, from Old French morir, from Latin morīrī, variant of morī.
Inherited from Old French ier, from Latin heri.
Learned borrowing from Latin possibilis.

more.definition: to play (engage in games or play); to play (produce music from a musical instrument); to play (a role)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French joer, from Latin iocārī.

more.definition: to ask; to request; to wonder
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂-der. Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁tder. Inherited from Middle French demander, from Old French demander, from Latin demandāre.

examples.text: Quelle belle journée !

translations.de: Was für ein schöner Tag!
translations.en: What a beautiful day!
translations.pt: Que dia bonito!

examples.text: La ville est belle au printemps.

translations.de: Die Stadt ist im Frühling schön.
translations.en: The city is beautiful in spring.
translations.pt: A cidade é bonita na primavera.

collocations: il fait beau — the weather is nice
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French beau, from Old French biau, bel, from Latin bellus.

usage_note: Goes before the noun: une belle maison.

more.definition: young; who has recently acquired a new status, who has newly become something (without being necessarily young in absolute terms)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French jeune, from Old French juene, juefne, from Vulgar Latin *iŏvenem, from Latin iuvenem.
Inherited from Middle French jeune, from Old French juene, juefne, from Vulgar Latin *iŏvenem, from Latin iuvenem.

more.definition: er, um, uh; expressing hesitation, reflection, confusion, or doubt

more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French dehors, defors, from Old French defors, from Vulgar Latin dē forīs, from Latin dē + forīs (“outdoors”).

more.definition: a doctor (physician); a doctor (person who has attained a doctorate), especially a male doctor
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin doctor.

more.definition: to call (out); to call, phone, ring; to call for, summon
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin appellāre (“to address, to call by name”).
Inherited from Middle French verité, from Old French verité, borrowed from Latin vēritātem. An inherited/popular Old French form verté also once existed. Compare English verity.
Inherited from Middle French eschole, from Old French escole, an early borrowing or semi-learned word taken from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).

more.definition: head; article, principal point; principal motive, charge, count of indictment
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French chief, from Old French chief, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *kaput-. Doublet of cap.

Inherited from Middle French sepmaine, from Old French semaine, from Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), derived from septimus (“seventh”).

Inherited from Middle French vivre, from Old French vivre, from Latin vīvere. Forms in véc- originate from Latin irregular perfect stem vīx- (vīxī, vīxistī, ...) undergoing metathesis and shortening to vĭsc-.

more.definition: fire; lighter, something to light a cigarette with; traffic light
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French fu, from Latin focus (“hearth”), which in Late and Vulgar Latin replaced the Classical Latin ignis (“fire”). Not related to English fire or German Feuer.
Capitalization of madame.
From télé- + -phone from Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, “afar”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “voice, sound”).

more.definition: near (a time or a place); close (to a time or a place)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French prés (“closely”), from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”) and pressus (“concise”), from premō (“to press, push, condense”). Cognate with Italian presso and Sicilian pressu.

more.definition: attached to, connects a person or an organisation delegated officially to a setting.
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French prés (“closely”), from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”) and pressus (“concise”), from premō (“to press, push, condense”). Cognate with Italian presso and Sicilian pressu.
Inherited from Middle French equippe, from Middle French equipper, esquiper. More at French équiper.

to gorge, to feed, to eat

translations.de: Was isst du zum Frühstück?
translations.en: What do you eat for breakfast?
translations.pt: O que você come no café da manhã?

examples.text: Nous avons mangé au restaurant hier.

translations.de: Wir haben gestern im Restaurant gegessen.
translations.en: We ate at a restaurant yesterday.
translations.pt: Nós comemos em um restaurante ontem.

collocations: manger sur le pouce — to grab a quick bite
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French manger, from Old French mengier, from Late Latin manducāre (“chew, devour”).

senses.gloss_en: to come, to arrive, to advance, to return
to make, to manage, to accomplish, to complete

more.definition: to arrive (often followed by a location); to happen (unlike other translations of happen, can be used with an indirect object to specify something/somebody affected by the action; it may also be used with a relative clause in the subjunctive); to cope, to manage
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French arriver, from Old French ariver, from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre. Synchronically a- + rive + -er.

more.definition: hard, tough (difficult to penetrate); hard (not soft); hard, tough (not easy, difficult)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French, from Latin dūrus.
Inherited from Middle French guerre, from Old French guerre, from Early Medieval Latin werra, borrowed from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”). Compare English war.
Learned borrowing from Latin secūritātem. Doublet of sûreté.

more.definition: boy; young man; man; Generic name of a male employee in some industries
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French garçon, from Old French garçon, garçun m (“servant, boy”), from Early Medieval Latin garciōnem, accusative of garciō m (“mercenary, servant, boy”), from Frankish *wrakkjō (“servant, boy”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, driven one”). Cognate with Modern German Recke ("warrior"), Old English wreċċa (“exile, outcast”), whence Modern English wretch.
From exact + -ment.

more.definition: strong; powerful; (informal) skilled, proficient, successful, sometimes translated "good" (often used in reference to academic subjects); who can count on
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French fort, from Latin fortem (“strong”), from Old Latin forctis, fortis.
Univerbation of près + que. Akin to Italian pressoché.

Inherited from Old French plein, from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Compare Catalan ple; Italian pieno; Portuguese cheio; Romanian plin; Sardinian prenu; Spanish lleno; English plene, full.

more.definition: behind; at the bottom of, behind (covertly responsible for)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French deriere, from Late Latin dē retrō, from Latin dē + retrō. Cognate with Italian dietro.
alternative form of bien
From marier + -age.

more.definition: last; latest (most recent); latter (usually preceded by the determiner ce); see: ce dernier
more.etymology: From a contraction of earlier derrenier, a derivation of Old French derrain (through analogy with premier), itself derived from Vulgar Latin *dēretrānus, from Latin dē + retrō + -ānus.
Inherited from Middle French fol, from Old French fol, from Latin follem. Cognate with English fool.

more.definition: to fall; to come down; to bump into, to come across; to be received by (when making a telephone call)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French tomber, from Old French tomber, tumber (“to dance, leap, do somersaults”), itself either of expressive/onomatopoeic origin (compare also Catalan and Portuguese tombar; Spanish tumbar; Romanian tumbă; Italian tombolare etc.), or alternatively more likely from Frankish *tumbōn, tūmōn (“to rotate, reel, sway”), from Proto-Germanic *tūmōną (“to turn, rotate”), of uncertain origin.

senses.gloss_en: to await, to expect, to abide

examples.text: J'attends le bus.

translations.de: Ich warte auf den Bus.
translations.en: I am waiting for the bus.
translations.pt: Estou esperando o ônibus.

examples.text: Nous t'avons attendu pendant une heure.

translations.de: Wir haben eine Stunde auf dich gewartet.
translations.en: We waited an hour for you.
translations.pt: Esperamos uma hora por você.

more.definition: to wait for, to await; to expect
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French atendre, from Latin attendere.

usage_note: No preposition for "for": attendre quelqu'un, never attendre pour.

more.definition: desire, lust, urge; appetite, craving; envy
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French enveie (with /ei̯/ modified to /i/ to match the verb envier), from Latin invidia.

more.definition: winter holidays (always in plural); party; name day
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁stosder. Proto-Italic *fēstosder. Inherited from Middle French feste, from Old French feste, from Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstum. Doublet of festin.

more.definition: game (activity performed for amusement); play (in a theatre/theater); set (of objects that belong together)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French geu, gieu, giu, from Latin iocus, jocus.

more.definition: land; region; home ground; homeland; home country; country; nation; country
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French pays, from Old French pais, from Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”), derived from Latin pāgus (“countryside; district”). See related terms. Cognates include Italian paese. Borrowed into Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish as país.

more.definition: stream of water, river; course (of events); teaching, lesson, lecture, class
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French cours, inherited from Latin cursus. Doublet of course and cursus. Compare Italian corso.
Inherited from Old French bientost. By surface analysis, bien (“very”) + tôt (“early”).

more.definition: number; phone number; issue (of a publication)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Italian numero. Doublet of nombre.

From Middle French cinq, from Old French cinc, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, dissimilation of Classical Latin quīnque (“five”), from Proto-Italic *kʷenkʷe, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe, cognate with Portuguese and Spanish cinco, Italian cinque. Doublet of punch.
Calque of Latin perfectus based on French par- + fait, inherited from Latin per- and factus respectively.

Inherited from Middle French ainsi, from Old French ensi, ainsins, probably from Latin ad (“to”) + in (“in”) + sīc (“thus”). Alternatively, from Old French ains + si, but this is less likely, especially for the forms beginning with en-. Compare Catalan així, Italian così, Portuguese assim, Romanian așa, Spanish así.

more.definition: punishment; psychological pain, sorrow; effort, trouble
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French peine, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Cognate with Spanish pena, Italian pena, Portuguese pena. False friend of Spanish peine (“comb”).

more.definition: minute (etymology 1, time unit, all same senses)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French minute, borrowed from Latin minūta. Compare menu, an inherited doublet.

more.definition: map (schematic maps of streets, subways, etc.); plane (flat surface); plane
more.etymology: From earlier plant, derived from the verb planter, or from Latin planus. Doublet of plant or plain, depending on which etymology is right.
Learned borrowing from Latin instans.
Inherited from Old French prison, inherited from Latin prehēnsiōnem, from prehendō. Doublet of préhension.

examples.text: Je pense souvent à ma famille.

translations.de: Ich denke oft an meine Familie.
translations.en: I often think of my family.
translations.pt: Eu penso muito na minha família.

examples.text: Que penses-tu de ce livre ?

translations.de: Was denkst du über dieses Buch?
translations.en: What do you think about this book?
translations.pt: O que você pensa sobre este livro?

more.definition: to think, reflect, concentrate one's mind on something; to think, imagine, believe; to be of the opinion that, believe
collocations: penser à voix haute — to think out loud
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French penser, from Old French penser, from Latin pēnsāre, whence also the doublet peser, as well as panser, originally an alternative spelling which acquired a special sense.

more.definition: to test, to try on; to try, to attempt; to try one's hand
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French essayer, essaier, from Old French essaiier, essayer, essaier, from essay, essai (“attempt; assay; experiment”) + -er (“infinitive-forming suffix”), from Late Latin exagium (“weight; weighing, testing on the balance”), from Latin exigere + -ium, from ex- + agere, from Proto-Italic *agō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti.

Inherited from Middle French arme, from Old French arme, from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).

Inherited from Middle French maulvais, from Old French malvais, malveis (“evil, wicked, bad, of poor or inferior quality", later also "unlucky”), from Late Latin malifātius (“unfortunate”, 4th c.), from Latin malus (“bad”) + fātum (“fate”). Cognate with Italian malvagio, and with Spanish and Portuguese malvado, all of them through Old Occitan malvatz.

more.definition: word; note, (short) message; answer to an enigma
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French mot, from Old French mot, from Late Latin muttum (“sound”), from muttīre (“mutter, make a mu-noise”), of onomatopoeic origin. Has almost entirely replaced parole in Modern French, perhaps because of its brevity. Compare Catalan mot.

more.definition: to work; to study; to struggle
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French travailler, from Old French travailler (“to toil, suffer, torment”), from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“to torture”), derived from Late Latin tripālium (“torture instrument”), from Latin tripālis (“having three stakes”).
Inherited from Old French quatre, qatre, catre, from Latin quattuor, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Compare Catalan quatre, Italian quattro, Portuguese quatro, Spanish cuatro.

more.definition: to go back, to re-enter; to go (back) home, to come (back) home; to get in, to go in, to fit in
more.etymology: From Old French, re- + entrer.

senses.gloss_en: to look, to gaze, to view, to see
to watch, to supervise, to observe

more.definition: to look at; to watch; to face
more.etymology: From Middle French, from Old French reguarder, corresponding to French re- + garder.

Inherited from Middle French choix, from Old French chois, deverbal from choisir, coisir (“to differentiate, see distinctly”), from Frankish *keusan (see contemporary Dutch kiezen), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- (“to choose”).
Univerbation of par fois.
Borrowed from English film.

more.definition: error, mistake; fault, blame; wrong, misdemeanor
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin *fallita, feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō. Compare Catalan, Spanish, and Portuguese falta. Doublet of faillite. Compare English fault and Spanish falta (“lack, shortage”).

more.definition: easy, simple; easy, promiscuous (consenting readily to sex)
more.etymology: From Middle French facile (15th c.), a borrowing from Latin facilis (“easy”), likely under influence of Italian facile.

more.definition: to exchange (something); to change (money, a job, one's circumstances etc.); to change, alter (something en into)
more.etymology: From Old French changier. Cognate with Norman changi, Walloon candjî.

more.definition: to hear; to be able to hear; to listen to
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French entendre, from Old French entendre, from Latin intendere (“to turn one’s attention, to strain”). Cognate with Catalan entendre (“understand”), Spanish entender (“understand”), English intend, Italian intendere (“mean”), Romanian întinde (“stretch, spread, extend”).
Inherited from Middle French plaisir, from Old French plaisir, from Latin placēre. Compare Occitan plaser, Catalan plaer.
From heur (“luck”) + -eux. Compare Occitan aürós.
Inherited from Old French propre, borrowed from Latin proprius.

more.definition: to keep; to retain; to store; to save; to guard; to be careful (de faire not to do)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French garder, from Old French guarder, from Early Medieval Latin wardāre. Cognate to English ward.
Inherited from Middle French agent, from Latin agentem.
Inherited from Old French lit, from Latin lectus.

senses.gloss_en: to come to, to reach, to pass, to pronounce

more.definition: to return, to restore, to give back; to repay; to reciprocate (an action, emotions); to render, to make
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French rendre, from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere.

examples.text: La route du village est très étroite.

translations.de: Die Straße zum Dorf ist sehr schmal.
translations.en: The road to the village is very narrow.
translations.pt: A estrada para o vilarejo é muito estreita.

examples.text: Beaucoup de routes sont fermées à cause de la neige.

translations.de: Viele Straßen sind wegen des Schnees gesperrt.
translations.en: Many roads are closed because of the snow.
translations.pt: Muitas estradas estão fechadas por causa da neve.

more.definition: road (sometimes route like "Route 66"); route, way, path
more.etymology: From Old French rote, from Latin rupta [via].

usage_note: For a street within a town, French uses 'rue', whereas 'route' is used for roads between places.

more.definition: place; locus (set of all points whose location satisfies or is determined by one or more specified conditions); outhouse, toilet
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French lieu, from Old French leu, from Latin locum, from Old Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”).
Inherited from Old French anee. By surface analysis, an + -ée; an (“year”) from Latin annus (“year”). Perhaps alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *annāta, from Latin annāre; compare Italian annata.
Inherited from Old French servise, borrowed from Latin servitium (compare Portuguese serviço, Italian servizio, Norman sèrvice, Spanish servicio), from servus.
Inherited from Middle French debvoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (to owe; ought, must).

more.definition: must, to have to, should (as a requirement); must; should
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French debvoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (to owe; ought, must).

Inherited from Middle French drolle (“a merry fellow, pleasant rascal”) from Old French drolle (“one who lives luxuriously”), from Middle Dutch drol (“fat little man, goblin”), itself from Old Norse troll, from Proto-Germanic *truzlą.
From Middle French difficil(e) (14th c.), a borrowing from Latin difficilis.

more.definition: subject (in a monarchy); subject; subject (topic, theme)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin subiectum.
Equivalent to ce + ci. See also -ci.
From im- + possible.
Inherited from Old French sorte, borrowed from Latin sortem. Doublet of the inherited sort.

more.definition: to lose (be unable to find); to lose (not win); to get lost
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French perdre, from Old French perdre, from Latin perdere.

more.definition: bizarre, odd, strange, funny; peculiar, quaint
more.etymology: Borrowed from Italian bizzarro.

From Old French tost, from Vulgar Latin tostum, from the neuter of Latin tostus (“toasted”), later meaning "hotly, promptly" in Vulgar Latin. Cognate to Italian tosto, Franco-Provençal toût, Catalan tost, Occitan tost, Walloon toist, Ladin tosc.

more.definition: to pay (for); to pay (someone); to buy (something)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French payer, from Old French paiier, paier, from Latin pacāre (“pacify”).

more.definition: Audio (France (Vosges)): (file); from […] onward; starting from; as early as, as soon as

Alternatively from a supposed Old French *seon, an old form of segun, son (“in accordance with”) (itself from Latin secundum; compare Old Occitan segon), later crossed with long, lonc.

more.definition: to have; to hold; to keep; to stay; to hold
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French tenir, from Old French tenir, from Early Medieval Latin tenīre, from Classical Latin tenēre.

more.definition: to want, wish, desire; to expect; to think; forms rhetorical questions, perhaps better translated to English by rephrasing with would or should; to see oneself as; to give the impression of, to seem
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French voloir, voleir, from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

more.definition: to read; to play; to be read
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French lire, from Latin legere, from Proto-Italic *legō, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-.
From Middle French doulcement, from Old French dolcement, dulcement, equivalent to douce + -ment.

more.definition: pretty; cute; jolly, nice, pleasant, agreeable
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French joly (“considerable, ingenious, agreeable, pretty”), from Old French joli, jolif (“pretty, smart, joyful, merry”), possibly from Old Norse jól (midwinter festival), from Proto-Germanic *jehwlą, *jeulō (“Yule, Yule month, December”) (more at yule); alternatively from Vulgar Latin *gaudivus (from Latin gaudeō, more at joy).
From Latin exāctus.

more.definition: to stop carrying, to put down (something or somebody); to ask or pose (a question); to land (a plane)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French poser, from Vulgar Latin pausāre < Latin pausāre, influenced in meaning by pōnō (especially its past participle positus). Compare Italian posare.
Learned borrowing from Latin professor.

senses.gloss_en: to abandon, to leave, to quit, to forsake

more.definition: to leave, to quit; to part with somebody, to leave somebody
more.etymology: From quitte + -er, or from Late Latin quietare (“acquit, discharge, release”), from Latin quiētāre (“to calm”).
Inherited from Middle French loy, from Old French loi, lei, from Latin lēgem, from Proto-Italic *lēg-, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s < *leǵ-.

more.definition: to know (of), to be familiar with (a person, place, fact, event); to know, to experience (glory, hunger, problems etc.); to be knowledgeable (en about)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French conoistre, from Late Latin conōscere, from Latin cognōscere. One of few examples where ⟨oi⟩ had been turned into ⟨ai⟩ /ɛ/ instead of /wa/ (alongside adjectival -ais and imperfect tense endings).

more.definition: letter (written character); letter (written message); the literal meaning, the plain meaning of something
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French letre, inherited from Latin littera.
Inherited from Middle French conseil, from Old French conseil, from Latin cōnsilium.
From English bar. Doublet of barre.

more.definition: normal (according to norms, usual); normal (relating to a school to teach teachers how to teach); okay, alright
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nōrmālis. By surface analysis, norme + -al.

more.definition: danger; jeopardy (danger of loss, harm, or failure)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French dangier, alteration of Old French dongier (due to association with Latin damnum (“damage”)), from Vulgar Latin *domniārium (“authority, power”), from Latin dominus (“lord, master”).
From Old French dangereus, from dangier. Equivalent to danger + -eux.

more.definition: aim; goal (result one is attempting to achieve); goal (in the place, act, or point sense)
more.etymology: From Middle French but (“mark, goal”), from Old French but (“aim, goal, end, target”), from Old French butte (“mound, knoll, target”), from Frankish *but (“stump, log”), or from Old Norse bútr (“log, stump, butt”); both from Proto-Germanic *buttaz (“end, piece”). Cognate with Old English butt (“tree stump”); see butt. The semantic development from "mound" to "target" is likely from martial training practice.

Inherited from Middle French froit, from Old French froit, freid, inherited from Latin frīgidus (“cold”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form frigdus, fricdus, attested in the Appendix Probi, or fridus, on a Pompeian inscription). Doublet of frigide, a later borrowing.

more.definition: calm, quiet, tranquil, still, peaceful, serene
more.etymology: From Middle French tranquille (15th c.), a borrowing from Latin tranquillis.

more.definition: class, type, group; class, cohort (all the recruits conscripted in a particular year); a period of military training
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin classis.
Inherited from Latin cunnus, probably ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin. Compare Persian کون (kun, “anus”).
Deverbal from visiter.
From Middle French preuve, from Old French prueve, preuve; synchronically derivable from the verb prouver. Possibly corresponds to Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.

more.definition: to forget; to leave something behind by accident
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French oblier, from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre, frequentative of Latin oblīvīscor (via its past participle oblītus).

more.definition: sky; heaven; canopy (of a bed, etc.)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French ciel, from Old French ciel, from Latin caelum, from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-.

translations.pt: Eu gosto dessa música.

translations.de: Sie liest abends gern.
translations.en: She likes to read in the evening.
translations.pt: Ela gosta de ler à noite.

more.definition: to love (usually of a person, otherwise the meaning is closer to English like); to like (often with bien)
more.etymology: From Middle French aymer, from Old French amer, from Latin amō (“to love”).

usage_note: About a person, aimer alone means to love. Aimer bien means to like.

more.definition: to listen; to listen to; to watch (a film or television)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French escouter, from Old French escouter, from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre. Doublet of ausculter, a borrowing from Latin.

senses.gloss_en: all the same, anyhow, anyway, nevertheless
all the same, anyhow, anyway, nevertheless

more.etymology: Univerbation of pour tant (“for so much”).
Inherited from Old French triste, borrowed from Latin trīstis. Old French originally had trist, inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, a variant of the same word.

more.definition: gullet, snout, face (of an animal); mug (a person's face); mouth
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French goule, gole, from Latin gula (“gullet”). Doublet of goulet and gollé. Cognate with Romanian gură.

more.definition: to smell (to have a certain odor); to smell; to sense, feel (physical perception)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French sentir, from Latin sentīre, from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to feel”).

more.definition: to open; to begin, to initiate; to open (of a door or a flower)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French ouvrir, from Old French ovrir, obrir, from Vulgar Latin *operīre, alteration of Classical Latin aperīre (“to open”). See also Italian oprire; Catalan obrir.
Inherited from Old French relacion, from Latin relātiōnem.
Inherited from Old French dame, from Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina.

Inherited from Middle French chascun, from Old French chascun, from Vulgar Latin *cascunum, *casquunum, a conflation of quisque unum (“each one”) + *cata unum, a variant form showing a derivative of Ancient Greek κατά (katá) (this variant form survived into Old French as chaün). Compare Occitan cadun, chascun, Catalan cadascun, Italian ciascuno.
Inherited from Middle French chanson f, from Old French chançon f, inherited from Latin cantiōnem f (“song, singing”).

more.definition: to fly through the air; to pursue flying; to scarper, flee
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French voler, from Latin volāre. Displaced Old French rober (unrelated to Modern French rober (“to wrap a cigar in a sheet of tobacco”)).

more.definition: white color; blank, unused; blank, without expression
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French blanc, from Old French blanc, branc, from Early Medieval Latin blancus, a borrowing of Frankish *blank, from Proto-Germanic *blankaz (“bright, shining, blinding, white”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”).

more.definition: certain, guaranteed (sure, positive); certain (specified, particular); certain (of indefinite, unknown or simply unmentioned identity, quality or quantity) (prepositive to the noun it modifies, and usually preceded by an indefinite article)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French certain, from Vulgar Latin unattested form *certānus, extended form of Latin certus (“fixed, resolved, certain”).

more.definition: soul; soul, heart, mind; soul, person
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French ame, amme, from Old French ame, anme, anima, from Latin anima. Compare dialectal English onde (“breath”), Gothic 𐌰𐌷𐌼𐌰 (ahma, “spirit”).

senses.gloss_en: cop, constable, police constable, police officer

more.etymology: From earlier flique, probably a borrowing of German Flick, German criminal slang for "young man". Alternatively, from earlier fligue, short for earlier fligman, a borrowing of German Fliege (“policeman”, literally “fly”). More at English fly.

Borrowed from Latin dēcīsiōnem (“agreement; settlement”). Cognate with Catalan decisió, Italian decisione, Occitan decision, Portuguese decisão, Romanian decizie, Sardinian detzisione, Sicilian dicisioni, Spanish decisión.

Inherited from Middle French compaignie, from Old French compaignie, from compain + -ie or alternatively from compagne, from Vulgar Latin *compania, from Late Latin compāniō, from Latin cum + pānis (“bread”). See also copain, compagnon.
Nominalization of the above verb.
Learned borrowing from Latin differēns.

more.definition: taffy, especially maple taffy; car; tire, tyre (of a car, truck, etc)
more.etymology: Deverbal from tirer.

more.definition: key (device for unlocking); key (essential attribute); wrench, spanner
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French clef, from Old French clef, from Latin clāvis, from Proto-Italic *klāwis, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kleh₂w-. According to Bescherelle, the spelling clé had replaced clef by 1845.
Inherited from Old French enfer, from Latin īnfernus.
Inherited from Old French vendre, from Latin vēndere. Cognate with Italian vendere, Spanish vender
Univerbation of lieu tenant, literally “placeholder”, from tenir lieu (“to hold the place of someone, to act as a substitute for someone”).
From Middle French estrange, from Old French estrange, from Latin extrāneus.
Inherited from Middle French diable, from Old French diable, deable, a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin or Late Latin diabolus, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

senses.gloss_en: to go, to extend, to reach

more.definition: to go up, to climb (go to a higher position); to ascend, go higher, go uphill, go upstairs; to get on, get in (a vehicle)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French monter, from Old French monter, from Vulgar Latin *montāre, from Latin montem (“mountain”).

more.definition: inside there; in this affair, (having to do) with this
more.etymology: From là + dedans.

more.etymology: Attested in Old French as enmener. By surface analysis, en- + mener.
Inherited from Middle French escrire, from Old French escrire, escrivre, from Latin scrībere.
Inherited from Middle French bouche, from Old French boche, buche, from Latin bucca. Doublet of bouque.
Inherited from Old French coupable, from Ecclesiastical Latin culpābilis (“culpable”), derived from culpa.
Inherited from Middle French rire, from Old French rire, from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre. The past participle's root-final S was lost.

Inherited from Middle French soin, from Old French soing (“care”), from Frankish *sunnija (“worry, care, concern”), from Proto-Germanic *sunjō, *sunþijō (“truth, care, responsibility”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sónts (“being, true”), from *h₁es- (“to be”). Cognate with Old High German sunna, sunne (“truth, need, necessity, apology, justification”), Old Norse syn (“denial”), Gothic 𐍃𐌿𐌽𐌾𐌰 (sunja, “truth”).
Borrowed from Italian appartamento, from Spanish apartamiento.
Inherited from Old French prochain, from Vulgar Latin *propeānus, derived from Latin prope (“near”). Cognate with Sardinian probianu.

more.definition: pouch, especially for tobacco; joke; a penis
more.etymology: 18th century, from Dutch balg. The sense “joke” (ca. 1800) from the notion of something puffed up, hence vain, fanciful.

more.definition: way, track; lane (of a highway); calling, path in life
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French voie, veie, inherited from Latin via. Doublet of via. Unrelated to voir and voirie, despite influencing the latter.

more.definition: horse; ellipsis of cheval-vapeur (“horsepower”); ellipsis of cheval fiscal (“tax horsepower”)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French cheval, from Old French cheval, from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin.

more.definition: combat (hostile interaction); combat (contest; competition); battle; military combat
more.etymology: Deverbal from combattre.
From Latin silentium (“silence”).
Inherited from Middle French tel, from Old French tel, tal, from Latin tālis. Compare Spanish tal.
Inherited from Middle French tel, from Old French tel, tal, from Latin tālis. Compare Spanish tal.

Inherited from Old French cachier, from Vulgar Latin *coacticāre, from Latin coactāre.
Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂-der. Proto-Indo-European *dʰéh₁tder. Latin mandōinflu. French commanderder. Present participle of commander.

more.definition: socket, wall socket (also prise électrique); hold; hold (of a climbing wall)
more.etymology: From Old French prise.
From gouverner (“to govern; to steer”) + -ment.
Inherited from Old French journal (“daily”), from Latin diurnālis, from diurnus (“of the day”), from diēs (“day”).

more.definition: contact; contact (with another person); contact (person that one knows); rapport
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin contactus.

senses.gloss_en: to take, to take over, to assume

more.definition: to get back, to recover, to recuperate; to reform, to rehabilitate; to reclaim, to recover
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin recuperāre. Doublet of recouvrer, which was inherited.

more.definition: base (bottom part of something); base (safe place); base, basis (fundamental belief)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).

more.definition: skin of a person or animal; hide, fur; skin (protective outer layer of a plant or fruit)
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French peau, from Old French pel, from Latin pellem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).

more.definition: to serve (to help in a shop; to bring a meal to someone); to be used for; to be useful, to be of use, come in handy
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French servir, from Old French servir, from Latin servīre.

more.definition: people (nation, distinct ethnic group); the people, the general population, the common folk
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French peuple, from Old French pueple, semi-learned form of pueble, from earliest Old French poblo (9th c.), from Latin populus, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”). Doublet of people and pueblo.
Borrowed from Latin exemplum. Displaced Old French essainple.
Univerbation of le (“the”) + quel (“which”).
Inherited from Middle French societé, from Old French societé, borrowed from Latin societātem (“society”), from socius. Compare the inherited Old French doublet soisté.
Inherited from Middle French sept, from Old French set, from Latin septem (“seven”), from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

more.definition: open; switched on; of a building: having a door of a specified colour
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French ouvert, from Old French overt, from Vulgar Latin *opertus, from Latin apertus. Doublet of apert.

14th century, borrowed from Latin hērōs, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs). The aspiration is secondary and originated in the desire to avoid les héros sounding like les zéros. The related words remain unaspirated. Displaced Middle French heroe, borrowed from the Latin accusative hērōem.

more.definition: to throw; to throw away, to discard; to throw away, discard
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French jeter, from Late Latin iectāre, from Latin iactāre.

Inherited from Middle French biere (early 15th c.), a borrowing from Middle Dutch bier and/or Middle High German bier, both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *beuzą. See beer for more. Displaced cervoise.
Inherited from Latin assessus.

more.definition: dress, frock; fur, coat (of an animal); wine's colour
more.etymology: Inherited from Old French, from Proto-Germanic *raubō (“booty”), later "stolen clothing".

more.definition: to reply, to answer; to answer for
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French respondre, from Old French respondre, from Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre.
Inherited from Old French horrible, orrible, orible, borrowed from Latin horribilis.
Inherited from Middle French vin, from Old French vin, from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.
Inherited from Middle French nez, from Old French nés, from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Compare Italian naso.
Deverbal from excuser.
Inherited from Old French environ (“around”), from en (“in”) + viron (“a turn”), from virer (“to turn, veer”), whence also French virer.
Inherited from Middle French terrible, from Old French terrible, from Latin terribilis.
Inherited from Old French posicion, borrowed from Latin positiōnem.
From Middle French, from Old French humain, umain, from Latin humanus (“of or belonging to a man, human, humane”), from homo (“man, human”).
From the expression temps à venir ("time (that is) to come"). Cf. also Old French avenir.

Inherited from Old French norriture, from Latin nūtrītūra (“act of feeding or nourishing”) and remade after the verb nourrir.

Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Old French tas (“heap, mass”), from Frankish *tas (“mass”), from Proto-Germanic *tassaz (“heap, mow”), from Proto-Indo-European *dāy- (“to divide, split, section, part, separate”). From Middle French banque, from Italian banca (“counter, moneychanger's table”), from Old High German bank, banch, banc (“counter, bench”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench, counter”).

more.definition: experiment, trial, test; experience (something one goes through); experience, knowledge and skills
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin experientia.

more.etymology: Borrowed from Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (tê). Compare Spanish té. Doublet of chai.
Inherited from Middle French mur, from Old French mur, from Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Italic *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).
From deux + -ième.

more.etymology: Inherited from Middle French baiser, from Old French baisier, from Latin bāsiāre (“to kiss”). As far as the verb is concerned, the meaning “fuck” arose via euphemism and has become the dominant sense. The noun derives from the verb.
Proto-Indo-European *Hróth₂eh₂der. Latin rotader. Medieval Latin rolluslbor. Inherited from Middle French rolle, from Old French role.

Learned borrowing from Latin evidentem.

more.definition: to attack; to diminish; to spoil; to erode; to begin; to undertake (an enterprise, an endeavor, a task)
